title: Anatomy of a URL
summary: A URL identifies a resource and where to find it: scheme, host, port, path, query and fragment.

sections.definition: A URL identifies a resource and where to find it: scheme://host:port/path?query#fragment. The fragment never travels to the server; everything else does.
sections.analogy: A full postal address: the scheme is the delivery method (regular or registered mail), the host is the building, the port the service window, the path the apartment, the query the extra instructions ("deliver only in the morning") and the fragment a note you use when you arrive, but the mail carrier never reads.
sections.problem: Knowing which part to use defines your API design: the path identifies the resource (/productos/42) and the query filters it or changes the view (?categoria=cafe). If you mix up their roles you end up with paths like /productos/categoria/cafe/orden/precio, impossible to combine.
sections.code:wire:
URL: https://api.tienda.co:443/v1/productos?categoria=cafe&orden=-precio#reseñas

# Lo que realmente viaja por la red:
GET /v1/productos?categoria=cafe&orden=-precio HTTP/1.1
Host: api.tienda.co
# El "#reseñas" nunca sale del navegador.
sections.code:server:
@app.get("/v1/productos")
def listar_productos(categoria: str | None = None,   # query param opcional
                     orden: str = "nombre"):          # query param con default
    ...

@app.get("/v1/productos/{producto_id}")              # path param
def obtener_producto(producto_id: int): ...
sections.bad:
GET /v1/productos/buscar/cafe/barato
GET /v1/getProductoById?id=42
sections.good:
GET /v1/productos?categoria=cafe&precio_max=40000
GET /v1/productos/42
sections.bridge:typescript: The fragment is exactly what SPA routers used in hash mode (/#/pedidos): since the server never sees it, it always served the same index.html. With normal routes (the router of an SPA) the server does receive /pedidos, and that is why you have to configure it to return index.html for any route.
sections.interview: A URL has a scheme, which indicates the protocol; a host, which is the domain; a port, which if omitted is 80 for HTTP or 443 for HTTPS; a path, which identifies the resource; a query string, with key-value parameters to filter or paginate; and a fragment, which only the browser uses and is never sent to the server. In REST design, the path identifies the resource and the query modifies the view of the collection.
sections.myths:
• Putting sensitive data in the query string: it ends up in server logs, proxy logs and browser history, even if you use HTTPS.
  • Believing the fragment reaches the backend.
  • Forgetting to encode special characters: a space travels as %20 and ñ as %C3%B1.
